stages.name: Capitalism and inequality
stages.title: Capitalism and inequality
stages.sub: How the drive for profit under capitalism tends to concentrate wealth, and why growth can still raise living standards.

steps.q: A factory owner in a private-ownership, free-market system keeps whatever money is left after paying wages and costs. What will they try to do with their capital?
steps.right: Use it to earn as much profit as possible
steps.wrong: Use it to pay workers as much as possible
steps.hint: Under private ownership, whose gain is the owner chasing?

steps.q: An owner reinvests their profits into more machines and shares each year, while a worker's pay rises roughly in line with the economy. Over many years, which pot is likely to grow faster: the owner's capital, or the worker's wages?
steps.hint: One pot is compounding profits on profits; the other is just tracking overall pay growth.

steps.q: If capital keeps growing faster than wages, and people also inherit assets or already own unequal amounts of property and shares, what happens to the gap between owners and workers over time?
steps.hint: Faster-growing capital plus unequal starting assets, repeated year after year: does the gap shrink, stay put, or grow?

steps.q: The same profit motive that concentrates wealth also pushes firms to invent cheaper, better products to beat rivals and earn more. Even if the rich-poor gap widens, could ordinary people's living standards still rise in absolute terms because of this competition?
steps.right: Yes, absolute living standards can still rise
steps.wrong: No, if the gap widens nobody else can gain
steps.hint: Think of a worker today with a smartphone and cheap flights, versus a worker a century ago: relative gap aside, has their standard of living moved?
